title: How do you film yourself for a business video?
answer: To film yourself well, shoot horizontally with the camera at eye level, sit centered in front of a clean background, and face a window or soft light. Use a teleprompter app so you keep eye contact with the lens, record one or two lines per take, and keep the camera rolling between takes. Wear solid colours, and push your gestures and expressions a notch further than feels natural.
author: Ademola Adelakun

body.text: Can you film a good business video by yourself?

Yes. A phone or a decent webcam, a window and a quiet room are enough for a talking-head video your buyers will take seriously, as long as you get a handful of basics right. Filming yourself is easier than most executives expect, and it means you can record between meetings instead of booking a crew.

The rules below are the ones we give every executive before they film at home or in the office. None of them takes long. Together they're the difference between footage an editor can make great and footage they can only make passable.
What equipment do you need to film yourself?

You need a camera, a way to keep it steady at eye level, light on your face and a microphone close to your mouth. A recent phone on a small tripod covers the first two. A window covers the light. A clip-on lavalier mic is the one purchase most people should make first, because viewers forgive average video far more readily than bad audio.
If you want specific products at three budgets, our [recommended video gear list](/playbook/video-gear-list) has them.
Should you use a teleprompter?

A teleprompter is optional but helps most people. It keeps you on script and lets you hold eye contact with the lens, which is what makes a talking-head video feel like a conversation. A phone app such as [Teleprompter for Video](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/teleprompter-for-video/id1139307843) scrolls your script right next to the camera.

items.label: Reading off to the side
items.text: If you'd rather read from a screen beside the camera, keep it as close to the lens as you can. AI eye-contact correction can fix a small offset, but it has a limit.

items.label: Scroll speed
items.text: Set it slower than you think. You can always speed up, and a rushed read sounds like a rushed read.

items.label: Your words
items.text: Write the script the way you talk. Our [video scripting checklist](/playbook/video-script-checklist) helps you tighten it before you sit down.

body.text: Should you film horizontally or vertically?

Film horizontally. A horizontal frame gives your editor more space to work with: they can reframe, punch in for emphasis and still cut a vertical version for LinkedIn or Reels from the same footage. A vertical recording can't be turned into a good horizontal one.
How should you frame yourself on camera?

Sit in the middle of the frame with the camera at eye level and a clean or symmetrical background behind you. Leave a little space above your head and frame from roughly mid-chest up, so your hands show when you gesture.

items.label: Eye level
items.text: Stack books under a laptop or raise the tripod until the lens is level with your eyes. A camera looking up at you is the most common mistake in home recordings.

items.label: Background
items.text: A tidy bookshelf, a plain wall with one object, or a symmetrical office corner all work. Remove anything with readable text you wouldn't want on screen.

items.label: Depth
items.text: If you can, sit a few feet away from the wall behind you. It separates you from the background and makes the shot look less flat.

items.label: In the office
items.text: Pick a meeting room over an open floor. Glass walls reflect light and people walking past will pull attention.

body.text: How do you get good light and sound at home or in the office?

Face a window for light and record in the quietest, softest room you have for sound. Light from in front of you flatters your face; light from behind turns you into a silhouette, so never sit with a window at your back.

items.label: Light
items.text: Turn off overhead lights if they cast shadows under your eyes, and avoid mixing daylight with warm bulbs. If there's no window, a single soft light slightly to one side of the camera works.

items.label: Sound
items.text: Rooms with carpet, curtains and furniture sound better than empty rooms with hard walls. Close the door and turn off fans and air conditioning while you record.

items.label: Notifications
items.text: Put your phone and laptop on do not disturb. One ping can ruin a perfect take.

body.text: How should you deliver your lines?

Deliver one or two lines per take and keep the camera rolling the whole time. Short takes keep your energy consistent and give your editor cleaner pieces to work with, and you don't have to memorize anything longer than a sentence or two.

items.label: Keep rolling
items.text: Don't stop recording after each take. Pause, reset and say the line again. One long file is far easier to edit than forty short ones.

items.label: Redo freely
items.text: If a line felt flat, say it again straight away. Your editor will pick the best one.

items.label: Mark the good ones
items.text: If you nail a line, say so out loud or give a thumbs up. It saves your editor time hunting for it.

body.text: What should you wear on camera?

Wear solid colours that contrast with your background, and avoid stripes, plaids and busy prints. Fine patterns can shimmer on camera, and loud ones pull attention away from your face. If your background is light, go a shade or two darker, and the other way around.
How do you look natural on camera?

Push your gestures and facial expressions a notch further than feels normal. The camera flattens energy, so what feels slightly too much in the room reads as natural on screen. Smile when you start a line, use your hands, and talk to the lens as if it's one specific person you like.

Most executives get noticeably better by their third or fourth recording, so don't judge yourself on the first one. If you're helping a reluctant leader through this, our guide to [getting your CEO on camera](/playbook/ceo-on-camera) covers the people side.
What should you check before you hit record?
Run through this list in the two minutes before you start. It catches nearly every problem that would otherwise mean refilming.

items: Camera horizontal and at eye level.
You're centered, with a clean background and a little space above your head.
Light in front of you, nothing bright behind you.
Mic on, close to your mouth, and recording (do a ten-second test and play it back).
Phone and laptop on do not disturb, door closed, fans off.
Script loaded in the teleprompter, scroll speed set.
Plan to deliver one or two lines per take and keep rolling.

closing.text: Once the basics are in place, the right gear is the next easy upgrade.
